summary: Comparing decimals that have the SAME number of decimal places (up to two) uses the same process as comparing whole numbers: work from the highest place value down and decide at the first place where digits differ. Because the numbers are equal length here, there is no ragged-length trap — correct place-value reasoning and an (incorrect) read-it-as-a-whole-number strategy happen to agree, so this is the foundational easy case. The genuine longer-is-larger / shorter-is-larger misconceptions only surface with unequal-length decimals (a later topic). The teaching aim is to build the place-value habit now, before it is tested by ragged decimals.
misconceptions: Reads the decimal part as a whole number ('72 > 27') — lands the right answer here but is a fragile, non-place-value strategy
Compares from the right (last digit first) as if column-adding
Ignores or misreads the whole-number part when it is present

activities.title: Order decimals on a number line and a length bar
steps: Take three cards — 0.45, 0.54, 0.39 — and place each on a number line ticked every 0.1 with minor ticks every 0.01, smallest to largest.
Say aloud why 0.54 lands furthest right and 0.39 nearest the start, naming the tenths: 'five tenths beats four tenths beats three tenths'.
View each number also as a growing length bar so the relative sizes are visually clear (0.54 is the longest bar).
Then place 3.72 and 3.27 on a 3–4 number line, first checking the whole-number parts tie at 3, then deciding on the tenths (7 vs 2).
State the order and justify by comparing the highest differing place first.
activities.insight: Decimal size can be read as position on a line: ordering is decided by the highest place at which the digits differ, read left to right, not by the raw digit string or the rightmost digit.

activities.title: Align place-value columns and read every digit by its name
steps: Write a pair such as 3.72 and 3.27 one above the other with the decimal points aligned vertically so equal places line up in columns.
Read each digit by its place-value name — 'three ones, seven tenths, two hundredths' — never as a bare digit string.
Scan from the highest place downward and circle the first column where the digits differ; declare that column the decider.
Compare 0.6 and 0.60: first write 0.6 as 0.60 by appending a trailing zero so both have two decimal places, then read the places (6 tenths and 0 hundredths in each) to show they are equal in value.
activities.insight: Aligning on the decimal point and naming each digit by its place makes the comparison a place-value decision, and shows a trailing zero can be appended (0.6 = 0.60) to equalize length without changing the value.

activities.title: Pairwise comparison and placement practice (scorable check)
steps: Choose which is larger: 3.72 or 3.27, and give the reason.
Place a given two-decimal-place value at the right spot on a 0–1 line.
For each item, say which digit you looked at first and why.
activities.insight: Equal-length comparisons can be done quickly and correctly by comparing the highest differing place, and the reasoning (not just the answer) should be stated.

checkQuestion: Give the child these cards: 0.45, 0.54, 0.39. Say: 'Put these in order, smallest to largest, and tell me how you decided.' Then hand them 3.72 and 3.27 and ask which is larger. Watch which digit they look at first and listen to the reason — do not prompt a method.
checkAnswer: 0.39 < 0.45 < 0.54 (decided on the tenths: 3, 4, 5), and 3.72 > 3.27 (wholes tie at 3, so the tenths 7 > 2 decide). Justifies by comparing the highest place first.
